content.p: On the afternoon of Thursday 22 January 2026, three people were shot dead in two places in Lake Cargelligo, a town of about 1,500 people in the central west of New South Wales. A fourth, 19-year-old Kaleb Macqueen, was seriously wounded. The dead were Sophie Quinn, her friend John Harris and her aunt Nerida Quinn. Police named the man they wanted as Julian Ingram, 37, a council gardener and Sophie Quinn's former partner, who was out on bail for domestic violence charges relating to her.

Ingram was never arrested and never stood trial. Hundreds of police searched for him for 109 days, according to the Illawarra Mercury, and on 11 May 2026 wildlife workers found a badly decomposed body beside his abandoned vehicle in a nature reserve. Police later formally identified it as his. Every allegation against him therefore remains an allegation that no court tested, and the questions that remain, about bail, about the search and about how he came to have guns, are for a coroner and a police review.
content.h2: The man police were looking for
content.p: Ingram, also known as Julian Pierpoint, worked for Lachlan Shire Council as a gardener, in a role described as weeds officer. Before that he had worked on properties to the west and north of the town, the mayor, John Medcalf, told the ABC. Locals told the Sydney Morning Herald he was an experienced bushman, and the ABC later reported stories of his bush skills and of weeks spent camping in the national parks around the town.

Police said he was known to them. According to Assistant Commissioner Andrew Holland, the head of the NSW Police Western Region, Ingram had "a long history with criminal matters", including similar violent offences, but had not breached any orders for five years. He had never held a New South Wales firearms licence.

The charges that put him on bail came from November. The Guardian reported that the offence date was 12 November. The Sydney Morning Herald said police granted bail on 30 November after he allegedly assaulted Sophie Quinn around the time they separated. He was charged with stalking or intimidation intending to cause fear of physical harm, common assault and damaging property worth less than $2,000. The Herald added charges of driving in a manner that menaced others and negligent driving. The Guardian reported that he had pleaded not guilty, and a hearing was set for 3 February at Lake Cargelligo Local Court.

Under his conditions he had to report to the Lake Cargelligo police station every day. On 3 December an interim apprehended domestic violence order was taken out on Sophie Quinn's behalf. It barred him from approaching or contacting her and from going within 100 metres of her home or workplace, and it was due to be reviewed on 3 February. Holland said a risk assessment had been done when bail was granted and had judged him suitable, because he had not committed a violent offence in five years. He said the court had left the conditions in place when the matter came before it three days later, and that police did not oppose bail at that hearing.

Police checked on him several times, Holland said, and found that he had met every condition. Holland said Ingram reported at 8.12 a.m. on the morning of the shooting. The Quinn family were not critical of the police effort to protect Sophie, the Herald reported. Parkes MP Jamie Chaffey took a harder line at the scene, calling for bail laws to change.

Police were called to Bokhara Street at about 4.20 p.m. They found Sophie Quinn, 25, and John Harris, 32, in a car with gunshot wounds. The Sydney Morning Herald gave Quinn's age as 24, and described the vehicle as a black Suzuki hatchback with bullet holes in its windscreen. A neighbour, Letitia Bardawil, told reporters she first mistook the gunfire for fireworks, then saw people trying to revive the two before family arrived.

A second call took officers to Walker Street, a two-minute drive away. There they found Nerida Quinn, 50, who died, and Kaleb Macqueen, 19, who had been shot in the driveway and was taken to Canberra Hospital in a serious but stable condition. A local woman who sheltered during the shootings told the ABC that children at the town pool had witnessed some of it. She said the man had fired from inside a vehicle while ramming into things.

Macqueen later told Nine News that he was outside a friend's mother's home when a gunman opened fire. "He was laughing," he said, describing the shot that killed Nerida Quinn. He said he had "terrible nightmares" afterwards. Holland said that all the parties appeared to be known to one another and that police were treating the incident as domestic violence-related. He told reporters that all the victims appeared to be related to the offender.

Sophie Quinn's family described her as gentle and kind. Her mother, Cathy Quinn, told the Herald she had "not a mean bone in her". Quinn loved fishing, pig hunting and her dogs, and she was due to give birth to a son in March. The family planned to name the boy Troy, after Sophie's father, who died when she was two. Her sister Tegan called her her best friend in an Instagram post that also mourned her aunt and her unborn nephew. The Guardian named a sister, Katy Quinn, as saying the family could have "no peace" while Ingram was free.

John Harris was, in a family statement read at Sydney's Invasion Day rally, a "proud father to three loving children" with an "infectious grin". Nerida Quinn was Sophie's aunt, a mother of four and grandmother of six, described by relatives as "selfless". A family friend, Leisa Kilby, told the Wellington Times that nobody prepares for three funerals, and set up a fundraiser for the funeral costs that stood at $17,000 of a $22,000 goal when the Wellington Times reported on it.

By Friday more than 100 officers were in the area. Specialist tactical police, negotiators and homicide detectives were flown in overnight with the help of the Defence Force. Holland said the town was not in lockdown, but The Canberra Times described deserted streets, drawn curtains and closed shops, and the Guardian reported that the IGA, the medical centre and the vet had been advised by police to stay shut. Premier Chris Minns declined to comment at length until the suspect had been caught.
The killings fell on a national day of mourning for the victims of the Bondi Beach attack of 14 December, a coincidence that the Albany Advertiser noted.

Police believed Ingram's local knowledge might keep him hidden for a long time. They searched villages and communities he was known to visit, including Murrin Bridge, about 15 kilometres north of the town, and two properties near Euabalong. On 25 January, reports reached police of a possible sighting at Mount Hope, a village on the Kidman Way with nine permanent residents. The ABC later reported that two girls hunting pigs there said they saw him twice in one night: first undressed in a paddock, then, hours later, raising a gun at their car. Police treated the sighting as unconfirmed. Heat of up to 45 degrees made the work harder, and the search area grew beyond 15,000 square kilometres.

Holland said police believed Ingram was acting alone but could not rule out help from local people. By May he said police no longer believed anyone had helped him to flee. Investigators weighed 300 public tips, according to the Illawarra Mercury, and police offered a $250,000 reward in March. Holland compared the task to looking for one person from a helicopter above the Sydney CBD.

At 3:40pm on Monday 11 May 2026, according to the ABC, police were told that National Parks and Wildlife Service workers carrying out feral animal control had found an abandoned ute in a nature reserve. Next to it was a very decomposed male body and a firearm. The reports put the place at about 50 kilometres north-west of the town (ABC, BBC and Illawarra Mercury) or about 100 kilometres north-east or north-west (AAP and The Nightly), and name it as Round Hill or Roundhill Nature Reserve. The ute's registration matched the one Ingram drove, and a council worker's licence and the clothing led police to believe it was him. Holland said it was unclear whether police had searched the area earlier, and that suicide was one theory under investigation. Police said the body appeared to have been there for some time, and the Illawarra Mercury reported that it appeared Ingram went to the reserve soon after the murders.

Two days later, police said the body had been formally identified as Ingram. They seized the vehicle and firearms for examination. "We had all intentions of bringing Julian Ingram before a court," Holland said on the day of the discovery.

Relatives of the Quinns were angry that Ingram would not face justice, a family friend told AAP. Sophie's mother Cathy called him "gutless", while Tegan said the discovery made it all feel real. Another relative said his death did not bring justice.

Investigations under Strike Force Doberta continue, and a report is being prepared for the coroner. Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said an independent investigation into the police search and a coronial inquest would inform changes to how police monitor domestic violence and bail. Holland said police were looking at ways to amend the bail considerations, and that Ingram's release had been examined in the critical incident investigation. In January, Holland said that how Ingram obtained firearms, for which he held no licence, would form part of the investigation.

For the town, the discovery meant, in Holland's words, closure and a chance to "relax". Lifeline Central West's chief executive, Stephanie Robinson, whose counsellors have worked in the town, said the perceived threat had affected people's feeling of safety, their moving about and whether children played outside, and that locals wanted Lake Cargelligo known for more than the killings.
